title: The Ruler's Table and the Morning After
sum: The "words of the wise" go on with advice for a young man at court. At a ruler's table, watch yourself and curb your appetite, because the food comes with a price (23:1–3). Do not wear yourself out for wealth that grows wings and flies off like an eagle (23:4–5). Do not eat with a grudging host who counts every bite (23:6–8), do not waste words on a fool (23:9), and do not move the old boundary stones to take an orphan's field, for the orphans have a strong redeemer (23:10–11). These sayings run closely parallel to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

Then a father speaks. He urges discipline, including the rod, which will save a youth from an early death (23:12–14). He longs for a wise son who will make his parents glad, and he warns against envy, drunkenness, gluttony and the prostitute's deep pit (23:15–28). The chapter ends with a comic and frightening poem about the drinker: bruised and bleary-eyed, seeing strange things, swaying as if at the top of a mast, and on waking already looking for the next drink (23:29–35).
readings: The sayings form a young official: how to behave at a great man's table, how to treat wealth and power, how to resist bribes and land-grabbing. Read this way, the chapter is about character in public life, and its warnings about appetite, drink and sex are warnings about the things that destroy careers and families.

23:1–11 follows the Instruction of Amenemope point by point, and 23:13–14 echoes the Aramaic Ahiqar. Read this way, the chapter shows Israel's sages at work: taking the best of their neighbors' wisdom and reworking it under the LORD, the redeemer of orphans.

At the center stands "Give me your heart, my son" (23:26). Read this way, the rod, the warnings and the drinker's poem are all a parent's plea: the father wants the son's heart, so that the son's life will make his parents glad (23:15–16, 24–25).

views.H: The setting is the royal court and the scribal class of Jerusalem: men who dined with rulers, managed estates and judged boundary disputes. Wine and mixed drinks were part of court banquets (Esther 1:7–8; Daniel 5:1–4), and boundary stones were a constant source of conflict over family land (1 Kings 21).
views.C: Critical scholars see 22:17–24:22 as a collection built in part on the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, with the clearest borrowing in 22:17–23:11, and a second unit (23:12–24:22) with no Egyptian source. The Old Greek differs often here, lacking 23:23 and reshaping 23:1–8 and 23:31; it may at points reflect a different Hebrew text.
views.W: Amenemope's chapters 6, 7, 11, 21 and 23 lie behind 23:1–11; the rod saying of 23:13–14 has a close match in the Story of Ahiqar; and Egyptian teachings such as Ani warn the young against the beer-house in terms close to 23:29–35.
views.J: Jewish readers have used 23:13–14 with limits set by the Talmud and Maimonides, have read the "redeemer" of orphans as God himself, and have found in the drinker's poem an argument for moderation rather than abstinence: wine is required at Sabbath and Passover, and drunkenness is condemned.
views.X: Christian readers have often heard 23:26, "Give me your heart, my son", as God's own call. The rod sayings shaped Christian child-rearing for centuries, and the drinker's poem became a favorite text of the temperance movement. Ephesians 5:18 echoes the Greek of 23:31.

deep.b: For Proverbs 23–24 the Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex, with its Ketiv and Qere readings. The Old Greek was checked in two forms: Rahlfs' edition, read verse by verse for the verses cited in the variants and notes, and Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus, with his notes on Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus, read for both chapters in full. The Latin is the Clementine Vulgate. The Syriac Peshitta and the Targum of Proverbs were not checked for these chapters, and no Dead Sea Scroll of Proverbs covers chapters 23–24.

The Instruction of Amenemope is an Egyptian teaching in thirty chapters, written by a scribe for his son, preserved on a papyrus in the British Museum and published by E. A. Wallis Budge in the 1920s. In 1924 Adolf Erman argued that "the words of the wise" (22:17) borrow from it. The notes at 22:17–21 introduce the parallel and the "thirty sayings" of 22:20. In chapter 23 the parallels continue:

  • 23:1–3 and Amenemope 23: eating before a governor, watching what is before you.
  • 23:4–5 and Amenemope 7: riches that make themselves wings and fly into the sky (geese in Egypt, an eagle in Proverbs).
  • 23:6–8 and Amenemope 11: craving another's bread, a block in the throat, and vomiting. Amenemope's chapter is about coveting a poor man's goods (Lichtheim's translation); Proverbs reuses the images for a guest at a stingy host's table.
  • 23:9 and Amenemope 21: not pouring out your thoughts before everyone.
  • 23:10–11 and Amenemope 6: moving boundary markers and cheating the widow's field.

What the parallel shows. Israel's sages knew and valued the wisdom of Egypt, as 1 Kings 4:30 says Solomon's wisdom surpassed it. The order of topics and some images are too close for chance. What it does not show. Proverbs is not a translation. It picks perhaps a third of its sayings from Amenemope, changes them (the moon god who fetters the land-thief becomes the LORD, the orphans' redeemer), and sets them beside sayings with no Egyptian source. Most scholars think the Hebrew sage borrowed, directly or through an Aramaic version; a minority, such as John Ruffle (1977), think both drew on shared scribal tradition. The parallel cannot by itself date the collection, and it does not settle whether Solomon or later sages made it. After 23:11 the Egyptian parallels stop.

deep.h: The rod: what the Hebrew says
deep.b: 23:13–14 is the fullest of the rod sayings (10:13; 13:24; 19:18; 22:15; 26:3; 29:15). The words are plain: do not withhold musar (discipline) from a na'ar (a boy or young man); "strike him" (nakah) with the shevet (a stick or rod, the same word as a shepherd's staff and a king's scepter); he will not die; you will save his life from Sheol. The rod was the ordinary tool of discipline in the ancient world. Egyptian school texts speak of beating pupils as a matter of course, and the Aramaic papyrus of the Story of Ahiqar from Elephantine has a saying almost identical to this one: "My son, if I beat thee, thou diest not" (in Charles's 1913 translation; see the note at 23:13). The promise is about life and death: a youth left uncorrected goes the way of the fool toward an early grave (5:23; 19:18). The Plain does not soften or update the text.

deep.h: The rod: how it has been used and read
deep.b:
In Jewish teaching the rod was accepted, and limited. The Talmud tells a teacher to strike a child only with a shoe strap (Bava Batra 21a), and it condemns a father who strikes his grown son, because it tempts the son to strike back, breaking the command not to put a stumbling block before the blind (Moed Katan 17a). Maimonides allows a teacher to strike pupils to instill awe, but not cruelly, and only with a small strap, never a stick or a whip (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Torah Study 2:2). Many modern Jewish educators read the verses as a call to firm discipline rather than to physical punishment.

In Christian history the rod sayings were used for centuries to justify beating in homes and schools. Augustine remembered the beatings of his schooldays and his prayers to escape them (Confessions 1.9). Puritan and later evangelical manuals made the rod a duty of loving parents. In the twentieth century James Dobson's Dare to Discipline (1970) taught measured spanking of young children, and many evangelical teachers still do.

Other Christian readers argue that the verses describe the practice of their time. William Webb (Corporal Punishment in the Bible, 2011) points out that the rod texts speak of beating youths, on the back, without limit on blows, which no modern advocate of spanking actually follows, and argues that Scripture's own direction points toward gentler discipline. Many churches and Jewish bodies now discourage or oppose physical punishment of children; others defend it as biblical. The New Testament keeps the goal while warning fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21), and Hebrews 12:5–11 speaks of discipline as a sign of a father's love.

23:29–35 is the longest poem in the collection and one of the most vivid in the Bible. It opens with a riddle of six questions (23:29), gives the answer (23:30), then a command (23:31), then the results: the snakebite (23:32), the strange sights and twisted talk (23:33), the swaying bed (23:34), and finally the drinker's own words, numb to pain and already wanting more (23:35). The poem is funny in places, but its point is grim: drink takes away the very sense that could warn you.

Egyptian teachers also warned young men away from the beer-house: the Instruction of Ani does so at length (Lichtheim's translation), and Amenemope has a one-line saying, "Accustom not thyself to sit in the beer-house" (Budge's translation, line 491). Elsewhere Proverbs treats wine more evenly: it is a mocker (20:1), it is not for kings (31:4–5), and it may comfort the dying (31:6–7). Wisdom serves mixed wine at her own feast (9:2, 5).

traditions.q: Does "Do not stare at the wine" (23:31) mean Christians should not drink at all?
views: No. Wine is a good gift and is required for the Eucharist; the sin is excess. The virtue of temperance calls for avoiding every kind of excess, including the abuse of food and alcohol (Catechism 2290).
No. Wine is used in the Eucharist and at feasts. The church's fasting rules give it up on many fast days as a discipline, which shows both its goodness and the need for self-control.

No. The Thirty-Nine Articles require that the cup of the Lord's Supper be given to all (Article 30), and the Church of England's Homily against Gluttony and Drunkenness condemns excess, not wine. Some Anglicans in the nineteenth century joined the temperance movement.

No. Wine is God's gift for gladness and is used in the Lord's Supper; Scripture condemns drunkenness, not drinking. Luther preached against drunkenness as a German vice while treating wine and beer as gifts of God (Sermon on Soberness and Moderation, 1539).

No. Calvin taught that God gave wine to gladden the heart (Psalm 104:15) and that Christians may use such gifts with thanks and restraint (Institutes 3.10.2); the Reformed confessions condemn drunkenness. Some Reformed churches have urged abstinence for the sake of others.

Many say yes, in practice. Wesley's General Rules (1743) forbade drunkenness and the buying, selling or drinking of spirits except in real need, and American Methodists led the temperance movement. Many Methodist bodies still commend abstinence as a faithful witness and use grape juice at communion.

Divided. The Southern Baptist Convention's 2006 resolution on alcohol cites 23:29–35 and declares "total opposition" to drinking alcoholic beverages; many other Baptists hold that moderate drinking is a matter of conscience.

Most Pentecostal churches, such as the Assemblies of God, ask members to abstain from alcohol, reading 23:31 as a warning to avoid the first step toward drunkenness and appealing to the believer's witness and to the body as the Spirit's temple.

echoes: 22:17–21; 22:28; 13:24; 22:15; 29:15; 20:1; 31:4–7; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 21:18–21; Jeremiah 50:34; Matthew 11:19; Ephesians 5:18; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:5–11

settings.what: Sayings on the ruler's table, wealth, the stingy host, the fool and the orphan's field
settings.by: the sage of "the words of the wise" (22:17), drawing, most scholars think, on the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope
settings.to: a young man being trained for service among rulers and officials, addressed as "you"
settings.when: as part of the thirty sayings (22:20); most date the collection to the monarchy, when Jerusalem's scribes and officials had contact with Egypt
settings.why: To teach self-control and integrity where a career is made or lost: at a powerful man's table, in the race for wealth, among stingy patrons, and in disputes over land. The orphans' redeemer (23:11) reminds the young official that the weak whose land he could take have God on their side.
settings.readers: For the later readers of the whole book, many of them far from any court, these sayings became general rules about appetite, greed and justice to the poor.
views: Most scholars, following Erman (1924), think the Hebrew sage knew Amenemope, directly or through a translation, and reworked it.
A minority, such as John Ruffle (1977), think the likenesses come from common scribal teaching rather than direct borrowing.
Many scholars think the collection was used to train scribes and officials, as Amenemope was in Egypt.
Others think it was meant for any young man of a landholding family who might rise in society.

settings.what: A father's call to discipline, wisdom and purity
settings.by: a father or teacher speaking as father ("My son", 23:15, 19, 26)
settings.to: his son, a youth (na'ar) on the edge of adult life
settings.when: in the second half of the words of the wise, where the Egyptian parallels give way to sayings like those of Ahiqar
settings.why: To win the son's heart (23:26). The father argues from love and from results: discipline saves life (23:13–14), a wise son gladdens his parents (23:15–16, 24–25), envy of sinners and companionship with drunkards lead nowhere (23:17–21), and the prostitute is a trap (23:27–28). Knowing that a parent speaks makes the rod sayings part of an appeal, not a rule for strangers.
settings.readers: For Jewish households after the exile and for the church, the passage became a model of parental instruction, and "Give me your heart" was heard as God speaking.

settings.by: the same teacher, now in a riddle and a dramatic portrait
settings.to: the son, and any young man tempted to drink late with friends
settings.when: in a society where wine was part of every feast and mixed wine was a luxury of the well-off
settings.why: To make drunkenness look as foolish and dangerous as it is, by showing it from the inside: the injuries he cannot feel, the visions, the reeling, and the craving that returns as soon as he wakes. The humor disarms the young listener; the ending frightens him.
settings.readers: Later readers used the poem in sermons on temperance and in Jewish teaching on moderation; it remains the Bible's fullest picture of what is now called addiction.

title: Rescue the Condemned
sum: The words of the wise end with more warnings and promises. Do not envy evil people (24:1–2, 19–20). A house is built by wisdom, understanding and knowledge, and wise guidance wins wars (24:3–7). Schemers and mockers are known for what they are, and strength that fails in hard times was never strong (24:8–10). Then comes one of the most searching commands in Proverbs: rescue those being led away to death, and do not say you did not know, for the one who weighs hearts knows and repays (24:11–12). Wisdom is sweet as honey (24:13–14). The righteous rise after falling seven times (24:15–16). Do not gloat over your enemy's fall (24:17–18). Fear the LORD and the king (24:21–22).

A short appendix follows, "These too are by the wise" (24:23). It condemns favoritism in court and the judge who calls the guilty innocent, praises an honest answer as a kiss on the lips, advises getting your fields ready before building your house, and forbids false witness and revenge (24:23–29). It ends with a story: the teacher passes a lazy person's ruined field and vineyard, learns from it, and repeats the warning of 6:10–11 (24:30–34). In the Greek Bible this appendix stands in a different place, between two parts of chapter 30.
readings: Much of the chapter concerns life in the gate, where cases were judged: plots and schemers (24:8–9), the condemned (24:11–12), favoritism, acquittal of the guilty and false witness (24:23–28). Read this way, it is a charter for honest courts and for the courage to speak up.

Envy, gloating, revenge and laziness are inner failings. Read this way, the chapter shapes a person who does not want what the wicked have, does not rejoice when an enemy falls, does not pay back evil, and does not let his life go to weeds.
Read as a book in the making
The heading of 24:23 and the Greek's different order show that Proverbs grew out of smaller collections. Read this way, the chapter is a window into how the book was assembled and handed on.

views.H: The city gate, where elders and judges sat (24:7; 31:23), is the setting of many sayings. Execution, judicial or political, could follow a hasty or corrupt trial (1 Kings 21:8–14). Vineyards with stone walls and terraced fields were the backbone of Judah's hill-country farming.
views.C: 24:1–22 completes the second, non-Egyptian half of the words of the wise; 24:23–34 is a separate small collection with its own heading. The Old Greek places it after 30:1–14 and adds five couplets after 24:22. Several sayings repeat others in the book (24:6 and 11:14; 24:20 and 13:9; 24:23 and 28:21; 24:33–34 and 6:10–11), signs that collections overlapped.
views.W: The image of God weighing hearts (24:12) uses the Egyptian picture of the heart weighed on scales. Ahiqar and other Near Eastern sayings counsel loyalty and fear before the king, as in 24:21–22. The farmer's field as a lesson is common in wisdom literature of the region.
views.J: The Mishnah gives 24:17–18 as the teaching of Samuel the Small (Avot 4:19), and the rabbis built on it a teaching against rejoicing even at the fall of Egypt. The Talmud reads 24:27 as an order of life and of study (Sotah 44a). 24:11–12 is read with the duty to rescue a person in danger (Sanhedrin 73a).
views.X: Christian readers hear 24:12 in the New Testament's teaching that God repays each by his deeds (Romans 2:6), 24:17 and 24:29 in Jesus' command to love enemies and not repay evil (Matthew 5:38–44; Romans 12:17–21), and 24:21 in "Fear God. Give honor to the king" (1 Peter 2:17).

deep.h: Rescue those being led to death (24:11–12)
deep.b:
These two verses press harder than almost anything else in Proverbs. Most sayings promise that wisdom pays; these demand action at a cost. People are being "taken to death" and are "tottering toward the slaughter", and the hearer is told to save them. The excuse, "Look, we didn't know about this", is answered with three questions folded into statements: the one who weighs hearts sees through it, the one who guards your life knows, and he repays each person by his deeds.

Who are the condemned? The text does not say. Many think of innocent people led to execution after a corrupt trial, whom an official in the gate could save by speaking (31:8–9; 1 Kings 21:8–14). Others think of captives or the oppressed, or of anyone in mortal danger; Jewish law draws the duty to rescue from Leviticus 19:16 (Sanhedrin 73a). What does it ask? Not that the hearer guarantee a rescue, but that he not hold back or pretend ignorance.

How it has been used. The verse has been cited for many causes; the anti-abortion "rescue" movement of the 1980s, Operation Rescue among them, took its name and language from verses like this one. Whatever the cause, the logic of the verse is the same: God's knowledge of the heart removes the excuse of not knowing. The Greek sharpens the excuse into "I do not know this one" (see the note on that phrase and the variant).

The command is clear: do not rejoice when your enemy falls. The reason is puzzling: or the LORD will see, be displeased, and turn his anger away from him. Read flatly, it sounds as if the hearer should hold back his joy so that the enemy keeps suffering.

Readers have answered in several ways (see the note at 24:18). Some say God's anger will turn from the enemy onto the gloater, since gloating is a sin. Some say the verse protects God's right to judge: vengeance belongs to him (Deuteronomy 32:35), and the human who celebrates claims a share in it. Some say the sage starts where the young man is and leads him one step at a time. The rest of the Bible pushes further along the same path: help an enemy's animal (Exodus 23:4–5), feed a hungry enemy (25:21–22), love your enemies (Matthew 5:44).

In Jewish tradition the verse is Samuel the Small's one saying in the Mishnah (Avot 4:19). The Talmud's story of God silencing the angels at the Red Sea, "My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you sing?" (Sanhedrin 39b; Megillah 10b), carries the thought even to Israel's oppressors, and many explain the Passover custom of spilling drops of wine at the naming of the plagues the same way.

deep.h: Where the Greek puts 24:23–34 and chapter 30
deep.b:
The Hebrew and the Latin give the end of Proverbs in this order: the words of the wise (22:17–24:22), these too are by the wise (24:23–34), the Hezekiah collection (25–29), the words of Agur (30), the words of Lemuel (31:1–9), and the woman of strength (31:10–31). The Old Greek, in Rahlfs' edition and in Codex Vaticanus, has a different order:

  • 22:17–24:22, the words of the wise, followed by five extra couplets about the king (24:22a–e);
  • 30:1–14, the first part of Agur's words;
  • 24:23–34, these too are by the wise;
  • 30:15–33, the rest of chapter 30 (the leech, the numerical sayings);
  • 31:1–9, Lemuel's mother's advice;
  • 25–29, the Hezekiah collection;
  • 31:10–31, the woman of strength.

Editions that number the Greek in its own order, such as Swete's, count the inserted passages as part of chapter 24. The Greek also hides the names: in 30:1 Agur's heading becomes "Fear my words, son", and in 31:1 Lemuel's becomes "My words have been spoken by God", which some think was meant to make the whole book read as Solomon's.

Why the difference? Scholars give three main explanations. (1) The translator's Hebrew had this order. The small collections may have circulated as separate units and been put together in more than one order before the Hebrew order became fixed. (2) The translator or a later Greek editor rearranged them, perhaps to keep the material of named non-Israelite sages inside the "words of the wise" and before the Solomon collection of 25–29. (3) Damage or copying of separate sheets. Some think pieces were misplaced in an early copy. Many scholars combine (1) and (2). Either way, the difference shows that the final chapters of Proverbs were still being arranged when the book was translated into Greek, probably in the 100s BC.

The book of Proverbs mostly states; here it tells. The teacher walks past a field and a vineyard, sees the weeds and the fallen wall, thinks about it, and "accepts its discipline" (24:32). Wisdom comes from looking at life. The lesson is the saying of 6:10–11, repeated almost exactly: a little sleep, a little dozing, and poverty arrives. The Greek turns the field into a simile ("A foolish man is like a farm") and the lesson into a confession: "Afterward I changed my mind; I looked, to choose discipline."

traditions.q: "Fear the LORD, my son, and fear the king" (24:21): must believers always obey rulers, or may they resist an unjust one?
views: Citizens are bound in conscience to obey legitimate authority, but must refuse commands contrary to the moral law or the Gospel (Catechism 2242). Armed resistance to oppression is allowed only under strict conditions: grave and lasting violation of rights, other means exhausted, and no worse disorder likely (Catechism 2243).

Luther taught that Christians owe obedience to temporal rulers in worldly matters, but that no ruler may command faith or sin; a Christian then refuses and suffers the consequences rather than taking up arms against the ruler (Temporal Authority, 1523).

Calvin taught that private persons must obey even unjust rulers and bear them patiently, but that lesser magistrates appointed to restrain kings may resist tyranny, and that no one may obey a ruler against God (Institutes 4.20.31–32). Later Reformed thinkers developed this into a right of resistance.

The Schleitheim Confession (1527) teaches that the sword is ordained by God outside the perfection of Christ; Christians obey rulers where they can, do not serve as magistrates or bear the sword, and answer injustice with nonresistance and suffering.

settings.what: The last sayings of "the words of the wise"
settings.by: the sage of 22:17, speaking as a father ("My son", 24:13, 21)
settings.to: a young man who will take part in public life: in the gate, in council, perhaps in war and at court
settings.when: closing the collection that began at 22:17; no Egyptian parallel in this part
settings.why: To steady him against envy of the successful wicked, to show that wisdom builds and strengthens, to forbid him to stand aside while others are led to death, to warn him against gloating and against joining rebels, and to tie his loyalty to the king to his fear of the LORD.
settings.readers: Later readers, living under Persian, Greek and Roman rulers or in the church, heard 24:11–12 and 24:17–18 as tests of conscience, and 24:21 as a call to loyalty that does not override the fear of God.
views: Many scholars read the whole collection as training for officials, which explains the attention to courts, war and the king.
Others see the "my son" address as a family setting, with the public sayings meant for every adult man in the gate.

settings.what: Sayings for the court and the neighbor
settings.by: "the wise" (24:23), an unnamed group of sages
settings.to: judges, witnesses and citizens who took part in cases at the gate, and anyone tempted to take revenge
settings.when: in a short supplement added after the words of the wise; in the Greek it stands after 30:1–14
settings.why: To keep justice straight: no favoritism, no acquitting the guilty, honest answers, no false witness, and no private revenge. The order to settle your fields before building (24:27) is a practical word to the same young householder.
settings.readers: For the later community, the sayings joined the law's demands for just judges (Deuteronomy 16:18–20) and became part of Jewish and Christian teaching on honest courts and forgiveness.

settings.what: The story of the lazy man's field
settings.by: a sage speaking of what he saw ("I went by")
settings.to: the young listener, and anyone tempted to put off work
settings.when: closing the supplement with a lesson drawn from ordinary farm life
settings.why: To show, not just tell, what laziness does: weeds, a fallen wall, and in the end poverty. The teacher models the wise response, looking, thinking and accepting the lesson.
settings.readers: The repeated saying (6:10–11) made the lesson easy to remember, and later readers applied the neglected vineyard to the neglected soul.
